prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and policy rules, which underpin the modern analysis of monetary policy.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B012 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. The round-1 exchange and the chair's questions did not give me a reason to change it. They did sharpen what I am claiming. The discovery I would credit is the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms and their integration into a microfounded framework for policy. It is not the whole estimated DSGE apparatus. Read that way, three contributions are separable and nameable: Calvo's tractable staggered pricing, which is the building block of the New Keynesian Phillips curve; Taylor's staggered contracts together with the policy rule, which gave nominal rigidity a dynamic form and a testable policy benchmark; and Woodford's synthesis into a normative framework for monetary policy. The work is 25 to 45 years old and has been through the 2008 crisis and the 2021-23 inflation. Those episodes led to modification and extension, such as financial frictions and heterogeneity, rather than abandonment of the core ideas. Under criteria applied equally across fields, I weigh conceptual centrality, breadth of influence on practice, and maturity, and B012 scores highest on those. I treat attribution cleanliness as a separate matter, and on it B012 is weaker than B026 or B007. I have not let the number of colleagues who prefer a candidate stand in for merit. No position has anything near six explicit supporters, and I do not want to move to a configuration I rate lower just to manufacture convergence.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and is the main reason my confidence is lower than my confidence in the science. Credit is spread over eight names. Any three-person cut omits Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets or Gertler, whose quantitative and empirical work made the framework operational. The Taylor rule alone is a thin basis, so Taylor's place depends on his staggered-contracts model, which is also a time-dependent mechanism. The micro evidence on state-dependent price adjustment that Friberg raises is a scientific qualification of the time-dependent mechanisms in Calvo and Taylor, so it counts against my own trio. The record after 2008 and in 2021-23 is contested, and the field is moving toward heterogeneous-agent models. Earlier prizes in monetary and macroeconomic theory overlap in subject, so the incremental claim has to be argued. B026 has cleaner credit and more than twenty years of firm-level testing. If the Committee gives attribution cleanliness decisive weight, B026 with Melitz and Helpman is a defensible choice, and I would not regard it as a weak outcome.

responses.point: Friberg names Calvo, Taylor and Woodford but reports a specific scientific reservation from his own price-setting research. Micro data from firm surveys and retail prices, including asymmetric adjustment, point to state-dependent behaviour closer to menu-cost models, which qualifies Calvo's time-dependent mechanism. He says he would not object to substituting Gali for Calvo.
responses.response: This is the most useful test of my own trio, and I think the critique is serious but does not decide the names. First, it bears on origination and on refinement differently. Calvo's mechanism became the standard building block because it is tractable and gives a forward-looking Phillips curve, and the state-dependence critique asks how good an approximation it is. That is a refinement question. Second, the critique applies to Taylor's fixed-duration contracts as well, and to Gali's New Keynesian Phillips curve work, which also rests on Calvo pricing. Substituting Gali for Calvo therefore does not escape it. Third, the critique does bear on how we word a citation. I would credit the foundational role of nominal-rigidity mechanisms and policy analysis. I would not credit Calvo-style pricing as an empirically settled description of price setting. I have not verified the micro literature independently, and I would defer to Friberg's expertise on how large the empirical qualification is.

responses.point: Andersson moved from Taylor, Woodford and Gali to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, regarding them as a separable lineage of pricing, contracts and rule, and integrated policy theory. He treats Gali as the natural substitute for Taylor if the Committee finds Taylor's contribution unpersuasive, and he qualifies the post-2020 inflation as a test of forecasting rather than a decisive test of the conceptual question.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of his argument and with the qualification on the recent inflation, which I read the same way: it tests forecasting performance and the framework's adaptability, and it does not settle the conceptual question. Where I would add something is on the Gali-for-Taylor substitution. I accept it as reasonable and said so in round 1. I would still keep Taylor, because his staggered-contracts model is an early and independent version of the nominal-rigidity mechanism, and the policy rule gave the framework a measurable link to central-bank behaviour. A Gali substitution would shift the citation toward empirical evaluation of the New Keynesian Phillips curve and away from origination. That is a coherent choice, but it answers the chair's question differently, and I would want the Committee to make that choice deliberately.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first. He holds that credit in B012 is widely diffused, that omitting Calvo or the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans work is a significant weakness of any three-name selection, and that the post-2021 record is unresolved.
responses.response: I accept the diffuse-credit point and have not found an argument that removes it, and I count it as a cost of B012 and not as something to explain away. We differ on what follows. I read the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans work as a distinct achievement: the empirical estimation and quantitative evaluation of medium-scale models. It makes the framework usable, but it does not originate its mechanisms. I would not combine it with the core theory under the three-person cap. Calvo is included in my trio, so one of the omissions you name is addressed. I also do not think the B007 pair dominates on scientific grounds. I agree its two-author attribution is cleaner, and I accept your point that the collateral channel is better established in theory and quantitative models than in direct identification. My own ranking of B007 was low largely because of the 2022 overlap. I do not claim that B012 is stronger on every criterion, only that it is stronger on breadth and centrality.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B012 sixth and treats it as an alternative. He argues that attribution across eight credited names is so diffuse that a three-person cut is arbitrary, and he would reconsider if the Committee settled the lineage question first.
responses.response: I take the lineage point as the key condition, and I think it can be met. The Committee can state which strand is the discovery: the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms and their integration into a policy framework. With that stated, the trio is not arbitrary, because each name maps to a distinct, documented contribution, whereas the estimation and quantitative strands are a different discovery that the cap leaves out. I do not claim this removes the problem. A reasonable person could define the discovery as the usable policy framework, and then the cut would look different. That is a judgement about the discovery and not a point of fact, and I would rather say so than present the trio as uniquely correct. If the Committee does not accept the lineage definition, your concern stands, and B026 is then the stronger option on attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the discovery should be defined as the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms (supporting Calvo, Taylor and Woodford) or as the usable policy framework (which would give more weight to Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler).
How far the micro evidence on state-dependent price adjustment weakens the time-dependent mechanisms in the proposed citation. I have not independently verified this against the literature.
How much the 2008 crisis, the 2021-23 inflation and the shift toward heterogeneous-agent models should reduce confidence in the framework's empirical record.
How much the earlier prizes in monetary and macroeconomic theory reduce the incremental case for a New Keynesian award.
Whether the attribution cleanliness of B026 should outweigh B012's breadth of influence if no position approaches six supporters. I do not claim to have settled this.
Whether the Persson named in my profile is Torsten Persson, which would matter only for B009 (see the conflict note).
statement.conflict_note: The chair asked me to clarify the identity of 'Persson'. My profile lists a paper on corruption as a collective-action problem with 'Persson and Rothstein' (Governance) and gives only a surname, so I cannot establish from the supplied evidence whether this is Torsten Persson, the B009 candidate. I have not verified it independently and I leave it unresolved. My round-1 withdrawal of the claim that Persson co-authored with me stands. If the person is Torsten Persson, that would be a co-authorship connection relevant to B009. B009 is only an alternative in my configuration, and I do not rely on it for my preferred part. I disclose it without adjudicating, and I ask colleagues to weigh my view of B009 with it in mind. My field is political science, with research on democratisation, quality of government and measurement of democracy. That is thematically close to B009 and to the 2024 institutions prize, for which I gave the presentation speech. That speech may reflect collective drafting and is not evidence of my preferences, and I do not treat my proximity to the subject as evidence of merit. No connection to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford or the other B012 names is apparent from my profile. At Stockholm University I am a colleague of Hassler, Krusell and Boppart, but in a different department.
